title: Wherever You Go in Queens, Diwali Fills Streets and Halls
excerpt: From 2,000 people at the Unisphere in Flushing to Liberty Avenue's motorcade in Richmond Hill, Queens celebrates Diwali on November 8 as a city school holiday.
body:
• Diwali falls on Sunday, November 8, 2026, and has been a New York City public school holiday since 2023.
  • More than 2,000 people gathered on October 10 at the Unisphere in Flushing Meadows Corona Park for the Arts4All Diwali and Navaratri festival, themed 'Unity through Light.'
  • Flushing Town Hall holds its 12th annual Diwali Festival on Sunday, November 1, from noon to 4 p.m., with children admitted free.
  • Reader utility: in Queens, head to Flushing for the Town Hall festival, Richmond Hill's Liberty Avenue for the motorcade tradition, and Jackson Heights for restaurants, sweet shops and festive storefronts.

Wherever you go in Queens this Diwali season, the festival is already there — in a park in Flushing, on Liberty Avenue in Richmond Hill, and in the restaurants and sweet shops of Jackson Heights. Diwali, the festival of lights, falls on Sunday, November 8, 2026, and since 2023 it has been recognized as a New York City public school holiday, a status the South Asian and Indo-Caribbean communities campaigned for over two decades.

Two Thousand People at the Unisphere

The borough's largest gathering so far came on October 10, when more than 2,000 New Yorkers attended the Arts4All Foundation's annual Diwali and Navaratri Festival and Parade at the historic World's Fair Unisphere in Flushing Meadows Corona Park. The free event, themed "Unity through Light," served more than 2,000 festival meals from different regions of India, and included a parade, Garba dancing around the Unisphere and a sunset diya aarti ceremony.

"The gift of Diwali and Navaratri is the power to come together and illuminate our communities by lighting the Diya lamp of knowledge, truth, and hope to give us the resilience and strength to overcome our challenges, differences, and inequities."

Dr Sumita SenGupta, the foundation's founder, said the celebration sought to bring communities together through shared traditions. More than 700,000 New Yorkers across Hindu, Jain, Buddhist and Sikh faiths observe Diwali and Navaratri, organizers said.

Assemblywoman Jessica González-Rojas told the crowd: "The South Asian and Indo-Caribbean communities' rich tapestry of cultures and traditions are what makes Queens so vibrant, and the Diwali and Navaratri celebrations have become an integral part of our shared communal life." Comptroller Mark Levine and Councilmember Shekar Krishnan also attended.

Flushing Town Hall: The Indian Wedding

The season continues in Flushing on Sunday, November 1, when Flushing Town Hall, at 137-35 Northern Blvd., holds its 12th annual Diwali Festival from noon to 4 p.m. This year's theme is "The Indian Wedding." At 2:15 p.m., Abha B. Roy and the Srijan Dance Company will reenact wedding customs including henna painting of the bride and the haldi ceremony, with audiences welcoming the bridal party in a tassa drumming procession.

Before the show, families can learn Indian classical and folk dance steps, try block printing with Dr Alka Mukerji, create rangoli art with Josh Roychowdhury, get henna designs by Bella Beauty and try Hindi calligraphy by Jasbir Bhatia. Queens Curry Kitchen will sell food and drinks throughout the afternoon, and Chef Nupur will demonstrate traditional vegetarian dishes. Tickets are $20 for adults and $15 for member adults, and all children attend free.

"Our theme for this year's Diwali Festival is the Indian Wedding, offering audiences a festive window into one of India's most cherished cultural traditions."

Flushing Town Hall executive and artistic director Ellen Kodadek said the festival reflects the venue's commitment to global arts for Queens audiences.

Richmond Hill and Jackson Heights

In Richmond Hill, Diwali centres on Liberty Avenue and the Diwali Motorcade, the community's longest-standing and most elaborate celebration, hosted by the Divya Jyoti Association since 1990. Floats funded by local temples carry children dressed as deities, dancers and musicians past spectators, while homes and businesses are decorated with fairy lights and rows of diyas — small clay lamps lit with a wick dipped in ghee.

"Back in the '70s when Indo-Caribbeans first landed here we had to hide and pray, we didn't have a temple. Now there's hundreds of temples. Now we can have a parade with thousands of people and we're able say this is our culture, this is our religion, and we can proudly share it with the world."

Lakshmee Singh, the motorcade's head organizer, told the Queens Gazette the parade "brings a sense of home to immigrants who have come from other countries, specifically from Guyana," with customs carried from Guyana — whose traditions originated in India — including sharing sweets such as gulab jamun.

Farther west, Jackson Heights and Richmond Hill are Diwali shopping and dining hubs, known for Indian restaurants, sweet shops and colourful storefronts, where families browse clothing and decorations and sample festive treats. With Times Square's free festival on Saturday, October 24, the pattern holds citywide: wherever you go, there is Diwali.
